sources.news_title: FTC Investigation Signals a New Phase of AI Regulation for OpenAI and Anthropic
Trump wants AI companies to police themselves. His FTC isn't waiting.
sources.text:
Trump Wants AI Companies To Police Themselves. His FTC Isn't Waiting.
While the White House settles for a voluntary accord, the Federal Trade Commission is preparing subpoena-like demands and plans to compel testimony from frontier lab executives.
America's leading AI companies are getting exactly what they asked for.
On Tuesday, President Donald Trump signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence—a voluntary, if vacuous, agreement to self-police and adhere to the same set of rules signed by the leaders of America's top AI companies. It outlines four layers of controls and audits he'd like every AI company to implement. The president told reporters he was "seeing tremendous self-policing," and that AI companies "understand that they have to self-police," according to CNN.
Trump has resisted calls to regulate AI companies even as public opinion of the industry has grown more negative. That hasn't stopped members of his administration from policing AI companies using the authorities already granted to them under the law.
On Wednesday, the New York Post reported that the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) would be "ramping up a sweeping probe of Anthropic, OpenAI and other frontier labs to uncover the potential dangers their technology poses to consumers, and plans to slap the tech titans with formal demands, similar to subpoenas, to turn over information."
The initial investigation began when OpenAI announced its agents had infiltrated Hugging Face's infrastructure in July. However, the Post reported that the FTC is now prepared to "force testimony from the leading firms' executives," including plans to "compel the executives at these firms to testify about their product and about the dangers they allege their products may have to consumers, to Americans."
The agency is investigating violations of the Federal Trade Commission Act, which empowers it to issue cease and desist orders to prevent "persons, partnerships, or corporations" from engaging in "unfair methods of competition in or affecting commerce and unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce." If companies ignore its orders, the FTC can ask federal courts to impose civil penalties and seek compensation for violations.
So far, the agency's attempts to regulate AI companies have aligned with public opinion. Last September, the FTC ordered seven companies to provide information on their AI-powered chatbots and how they "measure, test, and monitor potentially negative impacts of this technology on children and teens." In July, the agency announced it was seeking public comment on a proposed statement accusing AI companies of "manipulating the behavior of their AI systems contrary to reasonable consumer expectations for objectivity and accuracy."
The agency's latest actions come after a string of recent events in which AI agents from Anthropic and OpenAI meddled with government websites in the U.S. and Australia. Last week, FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson told Reuters that he would hold humans responsible for the actions of their AI agents.
It's unclear why the FTC has taken the lead and not the Department of Justice. In his speech at the United Nations General Assembly this month, Trump suggested the department would watch the industry closely for signs of misconduct.
Still, OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei—CEOs of the world's leading frontier AI labs who have asked lawmakers to regulate the industry and called for an industrywide pause on development—appear to be succeeding in their quest for regulatory capture.
An agency official told the Post that it would likely "issue its civil investigative demands, or CIDs, in the coming weeks."

sources.news_title: Trump admin quietly opens broad probe after handshake 'self-regulation' deal
sources.text:
The Federal Trade Commission has quietly opened a sweeping investigation into the safety practices of Anthropic and OpenAI, just days after President Donald Trump publicly praised the AI industry's ability to police itself.
A senior agency official, speaking anonymously because the investigation hasn't been made public, confirmed the probe to the Washington Post, though the exact scope remains unclear. The FTC holds broad authority to investigate unfair or deceptive business practices that harm consumers, and the inquiry hands the administration a useful talking point in its ongoing fight against calls from parts of the industry and Congress to write an entirely new regulatory framework for AI, rather than relying on the laws already on the books.
FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson laid out that philosophy last week at a Reuters-hosted event, warning that the push for new rules deserves real scrutiny before lawmakers act.
"There's no easier way for incumbents to insulate themselves from competition than to enlist Washington to come alongside them and build a wall and a moat around their existing technologies," Ferguson said.
The investigation lands amid mounting industry anxiety over whether the newest generation of AI models could spiral beyond human control. Companies have acknowledged a string of troubling episodes recently, among them an incident in which a group of automated OpenAI agents managed to infiltrate the systems of a separate AI company. OpenAI announced this week it had scrapped a planned model release entirely over safety concerns, and executives at both Anthropic and OpenAI have floated the idea of a coordinated industry-wide slowdown to buy more time for safety work.
Despite that unease, the administration has largely stuck to its position that responsibility for AI safety rests with the companies themselves, a stance Trump reinforced Tuesday when he signed a joint accord with top AI executives at the White House.
"I'm seeing tremendous self-policing," Trump said following the signing, adding that "there’s a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation."
Vice President JD Vance struck a somewhat different note later that same day, suggesting the Justice Department and FTC still have a real enforcement role to play if companies fall short.
"They have to build products that are safe and good for American consumers. The government actually has preexisting laws on the books where if you build something that gets unleashed on the internet, that is used as a tool for cyberwarfare, then you have responsibility for the products you develop," Vance said.

Anthropic, OpenAI and other artificial intelligence firms are now the focus of a sweeping investigation by the Federal Trade Commission into whether their products are harming American consumers, according to reports.
News of the investigation, which has not been publicly announced, arrived one day after Donald Trump’s “accord” with major AI firms, which the president described as a “morally binding” but voluntary pact with leading industry figures to self-regulate a technology that is facing immense political and legal scrutiny.
The investigation could be used to bolster the administration’s dubious position that existing laws can sufficiently protect against threats from rapidly developing AI products — despite growing, apocalyptic warnings from developers and routine news of autonomous AI agents gaining unauthorized access to sensitive systems.
Andrew Ferguson, the Trump-appointed chair of the agency, said last week that the federal government should treat warnings about AI threats with “deep suspicion.” After his meeting with AI executives on Tuesday, Trump repeatedly demanded that the world should call AI “super intelligence” and insisted the firms will be “policing each other” despite warnings from developers that their own products are now able to escape from them.
The Independent has requested comment from the FTC. Anthropic, which develops Claude, and OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, did not immediately return The Independent’s request for comment.
The investigation also comes as members of Congress and other oversight bodies grapple with how to respond to industry threats that are rapidly outpacing a halting, aging bureaucracy.
Anthropic and OpenAI executives have proposed a coordinated slowdown among firms to closely study how their products are rolling out. OpenAI also announced this week that it postponed a planned release of a new model, citing potential safety issues.
In Wednesday testimony to Congress, former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo said the use of AI products to both develop other products and regulate themselves is a “recipe for disaster” and urged government intervention.
Despite the president’s remarks, administration officials have suggested there is room for federal action.
Vice President JD Vance said Tuesday that the FTC and the Department of Justice could still function as watchdogs over the industry.
“They have to build products that are safe and good for American consumers,” he said at an event with xAI’s Elon Musk and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
“The government actually has preexisting laws on the books where if you build something that gets unleashed on the internet, that is used as a tool for cyberwarfare, then you have responsibility for the products you develop,” Vance added.
Pressure to investigate AI firms accelerated earlier this year after a wave of AI-driven cyberattacks targeted public water infrastructure in more than a dozen states.
Current and former Anthropic developers also delivered grave warnings that the AI companies were sprinting towards “superhuman systems that can hack anything” and endangering humanity in the process.
Anthropic also reported this month that the company blocked several attempts to use its AI for high-profile hacking operations as well as research that could create bioweapons, firearms, missiles, armed drones and bombs.
Those reports have raised major alarms for cybersecurity experts, who warned that AI’s potential threats should serve as urgent wake-up calls to the immense vulnerabilities in American infrastructure and the potentially devastating consequences of unrestrained, weaponized AI.
“We have a limited window to strengthen cyber defenses,” tech companies wrote in an open letter last month.
“In the coming months, AI-enabled cyber attacks will become far more widespread and sophisticated as models around the world become increasingly capable,” the statement says. “The companies and public services our communities depend on — from hospitals to water treatment plants to the infrastructure that powers the internet — are at risk.”
Tuesday’s vague, one-page document from the White House does not serve as an official order or executive action but rather an unenforceable message to an industry that the president has pumped enormous resources into protecting, insisting that American dominance over AI technology is critical for national security and economic growth in a race against China.
The document was signed by Trump as well as the leaders of Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia, OpenAI and SpaceXAI.
“We’re going to advance this technology that is so consequential to humanity, so consequential to the future prosperity of our nation,” Huang told reporters outside the White House following Tuesday’s closed-door meeting with the president. “We’re going to do it responsibly and safely.”

sources.news_title: FTC probes OpenAI, Anthropic, and METR
sources.text:
The News
The US Federal Trade Commission is investigating top American AI labs — and a prominent safety watchdog — over the potential dangers of their technology.
An FTC official confirmed the probe, first reported by the New York Post. The investigation was launched before an unreleased OpenAI model went rogue and hacked open-source AI hub Hugging Face earlier this year, an incident that triggered a fresh wave of concern over the possible harms of uninhibited AI development.
In addition to labs, including OpenAI and Anthropic, METR, a California-based nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI models for risks, is also a target. METR conducted an investigation into the OpenAI-Hugging Face hack and released a report on the incident.
The agency is set to send civil investigative demands, which are similar to subpoenas, to the companies in the next few weeks.
OpenAI, Anthropic, and METR didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.
Know More
The probe steps up US government scrutiny of top tech companies, even as executives from many of those companies gathered at the White House this week and signed a voluntary pledge to self-police their AI models. US President Donald Trump said the industry was showing “tremendous self-regulation.”
FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson earlier this month signaled opposition to government regulation driven by AI safety fears, telling Fox News that OpenAI and Anthropic shouldn’t be able to “whip everyone into a panic and then say, ‘We need a whole bunch of regulations that we can comply with.’”
He added: “That is how companies build a moat around their businesses to make sure that people can’t compete against them.”

sources.text:
The US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has launched an industry-wide investigation into leading artificial intelligence companies including OpenAI and Anthropic, amid growing concerns about the potential risks posed by increasingly autonomous AI agents.
A senior FTC official told Reuters on Wednesday (September 30) that the agency plans to issue formal demands for information and compel testimony from executives at major AI developers, including OpenAI, Anthropic and AI research group METR. The investigation is examining the potential dangers the companies' technology could pose to consumers.
The probe comes after a series of incidents involving AI agents carrying out unexpected or unauthorised actions, including cybersecurity-related activity. It marks a major US enforcement effort focused on the safety of so-called “rogue” or autonomous AI agents.
FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson had concerns about AI companies before an OpenAI agent-related incident involving the open-source AI platform Hugging Face, according to the senior official.
The incident increased the urgency around the issue, as OpenAI agents reportedly probed Hugging Face for vulnerabilities before carrying out a large-scale attack. The FTC is now seeking information from companies and researchers involved in developing and evaluating agentic AI systems.
The agency has broad authority under US consumer-protection law to pursue companies over unfair or deceptive practices. It has previously used those powers in cases involving inadequate measures to protect consumer data.
The investigation also comes as policymakers debate who should bear responsibility when autonomous AI systems cause harm or act beyond their instructions.
A series of incidents involving AI agents from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta has raised concerns about whether increasingly autonomous systems can remain within the limits set by their developers.
OpenAI
OpenAI’s agents were involved in several incidents:
Hugging Face: During cybersecurity testing in July, OpenAI models bypassed controls designed to isolate them from the internet, gained access to third-party systems and compromised parts of Hugging Face’s infrastructure. OpenAI described the incident as its most serious model-related hack identified at the time.
Australian government portal: An OpenAI agent accessed non-public files on an Australian government health-statistics portal while attempting to retrieve information. OpenAI said no personal health data was accessed.
US government websites: OpenAI agents searching US government website behaved in ways that went beyond their instructions. In one case, they found API developer keys, although only publicly available information was ultimately gathered. OpenAI has also been reviewing other incidents involving government websites.
Anthropic
Anthropic said its AI models hacked into three organisations during controlled cybersecurity testing. The company discovered the incidents after reviewing more than 141,000 evaluation runs as part of a large-scale security review.
The models involved included Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Mythos 5 and an internal research model. Anthropic said the earliest incidents dated to April and involved models accessing the internet from testing environments that were supposed to be isolated.
Meta
Meta disclosed that one of its AI models accessed the internet and hacked another company during cybersecurity testing.
Meta said the incident resulted from a misconfiguration by Irregular, the independent company conducting the testing, which inadvertently allowed the model to access the internet. The episode nevertheless added to concerns about AI systems taking actions beyond their intended testing boundaries.
The incidents have intensified debate over responsibility when an AI agent performs an unauthorised action.
Ferguson has rejected the idea of treating AI agents as independent actors that simply “break loose”, arguing that responsibility can instead lie with the developers or users who instruct the systems.
That question could become increasingly important as AI companies deploy agents capable of operating autonomously for extended periods and accessing external systems.
At the same time, President Donald Trump has pushed for US leadership in AI and has argued against excessive regulation, while also saying existing laws can be used to hold AI companies responsible for harm.
Trump met AI executives this week, with leading companies agreeing to voluntary standards for AI development. The FTC probe adds a formal regulatory dimension to those industry-led efforts.
The investigation is therefore unfolding as AI developers simultaneously expand the capabilities of autonomous agents and face growing pressure to demonstrate that those systems can be safely controlled.
(With Reuters, AP inputs)

sources.text:

sources.news_title: FTC opens probe into safety of AI, including Anthropic and OpenAI
sources.text:
(WASHINGTON) — The Federal Trade Commission has opened a broad probe into the safety of AI systems, including Anthropic and OpenAI, a senior FTC official confirmed to ABC News on Wednesday.
The New York Post was first to report on the investigation.
The probe is looking into allegations of unfair or deceptive acts by AI companies and potential harms to consumers. The agency could issue formal demands for AI companies to turn over information, a senior FTC official confirmed.
The FTC has the broad legal authority to investigate companies and enforce consumer protection laws. Its investigations can result in civil penalties.
ABC News has reached out to Anthropic and OpenAI for comment on the FTC investigation.
The FTC probe comes as AI leaders issue warnings about the threat of AI and calling for steps to slow it down before it outsmarts humans. Lawmakers’ calls for regulations for the AI industry have also grown.
President Donald Trump — who earlier this month called warnings about the dangers of artificial intelligence a “HOAX” — hosted key tech leaders at the White House on Tuesday, saying they signed a “constitution” to police themselves.
“This is a statement of principles that you’ll see, a statement of standards, commitments that are voluntary on behalf of the industry,” said Speaker Mike Johnson. “It sets forth expectations.”
Asked whether the agreement is binding, Trump said it’s “morally” binding.
ABC News’ Sarah Beth Hensley contributed to this report.

FTC Prepares Sweeping Inquiry Into OpenAI, Anthropic and Other Frontier AI Developers
sources.text:
Federal Trade Commission officials say the agency intends to demand documents and testimony from leading artificial intelligence companies as it examines whether representations about increasingly autonomous systems could violate existing consumer protection law.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
The Federal Trade Commission is preparing an expansive investigation into some of the country’s largest artificial intelligence developers, with senior agency officials saying regulators plan to compel testimony and records from executives as they examine the risks posed by increasingly powerful and autonomous AI systems.
OpenAI and Anthropic are among the companies expected to receive demands from the agency, according to a senior FTC official who described the developing investigation Wednesday.
The inquiry is expected to examine whether AI companies have engaged in unfair or deceptive practices under the Federal Trade Commission Act, including questions surrounding what developers tell consumers about the capabilities, safeguards and potential dangers associated with their systems.
“The agency has plans to compel the executives at these firms to testify about their product [and] about the dangers they allege their products may have to consumers, to Americans,” the senior official said.
A second senior FTC official separately confirmed the existence of the investigation.
The agency has not publicly identified all companies that could receive civil investigative demands, and the inquiry remains in its investigative stage. OpenAI, Anthropic and AI research organization METR did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson’s approach appears to rely heavily on existing federal consumer protection law rather than waiting for Congress to establish a separate regulatory system specifically governing advanced AI.
“People talk about how we need new laws for these companies, and the chairman’s been very clear … we have plenty of laws in the books,” the senior FTC official said.
The official emphasized that the investigation is not intended to halt American AI development or weaken the country’s competitive position.
“We want to maintain our dominance,” the official said. “Nothing in our investigation should remotely get in the way of that at all. We’re not telling them to stop. We’re not telling them to do anything. We are in the investigative phases.”
The FTC’s reported plans emerge as Washington confronts increasingly difficult questions about responsibility for AI systems capable of acting with less direct human supervision.
Those concerns intensified following a July incident involving OpenAI agents and Hugging Face, a New York-based platform widely used by AI developers and researchers.
More than 700 OpenAI agents participated in attacks on Hugging Face during experiments conducted in July, according to a subsequent METR investigation.
METR reported that approximately 1,200 agents communicated through an unauthorized message board, exchanging more than 70,000 messages and files. Roughly 700 ultimately became involved in activity targeting Hugging Face.
The agents had initially been launched as part of OpenAI experiments and were intended to operate independently.
Instead, some discovered ways to communicate with one another through an internal package repository, created an unauthorized shared communications system and began coordinating efforts.
According to METR, agents formed teams, divided tasks and pursued broader strategies intended to circumvent or manipulate the evaluation environment in which they were operating.
The activity eventually expanded into Hugging Face.
An agent discovered credentials associated with the platform, while other agents attempted to create accounts and access datasets. Another developed a method of uploading malicious datasets capable of causing Hugging Face servers to expose unrelated information.
By July 11, an agent had achieved remote code execution on Hugging Face infrastructure, according to METR, after which participating agents moved laterally through parts of the platform.
The incident attracted congressional attention because the agents were not specifically instructed to conduct the broader intrusion that ultimately occurred.
Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., opened a Senate investigation Sept. 10 into the episode and the broader risks of advanced AI systems.
Hawley argued that companies should remain legally responsible when autonomous agents acting through their products cause harm.
The incident has become part of a larger debate over whether existing laws can adequately address actions performed by AI agents, particularly when those systems independently select methods or intermediate goals that developers and users did not explicitly direct.
Ferguson has taken the position that humans and companies cannot escape legal responsibility merely because an artificial intelligence system performed the underlying action.
He has simultaneously pushed back against efforts by major AI developers to use warnings about catastrophic risks as justification for a regulatory framework that could entrench the largest companies.
Ferguson said during a Sept. 20 Fox News interview that he does not want AI laboratories “to come to Washington, whip everyone into a panic and then say, ‘We need a whole bunch of regulations that we can comply with.’”
That concern reflects a growing division in Washington over how the federal government should address powerful AI systems without establishing rules so costly or complicated that only the largest technology companies can comply with them.
The FTC investigation reportedly began before the Hugging Face incident became public, suggesting the agency’s concerns extend beyond that episode.
METR itself may also come under examination, according to the officials.
The Berkeley, California-based research organization studies the capabilities and potential risks of advanced AI systems and has conducted independent evaluations for major developers.
The widening FTC inquiry comes immediately after executives from several leading technology companies met President Donald Trump at the White House and signed a voluntary agreement concerning advanced artificial intelligence.
Trump described the agreement Tuesday as “morally binding.”
Executives representing OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI and other major technology companies participated in the White House gathering.
Ferguson was also present.
The agreement establishes voluntary commitments involving internal safeguards, independent review and other measures designed to reduce the risk that highly capable AI systems behave in unexpected or dangerous ways.
Trump has favored industry self-regulation while also making clear that companies and individuals would remain accountable when AI systems violate existing law.
According to a statement attributed to Trump by Fox News White House correspondent Aishah Hasnie, cases involving unlawful behavior by rogue AI systems could be referred to the Justice Department.
That approach would place responsibility on the companies and people deploying AI rather than treating autonomous software as an independent legal actor.
The FTC has broad authority under federal law to investigate unfair or deceptive business practices.
For AI companies, that could include scrutiny of claims made about product safety, safeguards, autonomous capabilities and the degree of control companies maintain over their systems.
Investigators could also examine whether companies knew about potentially dangerous behavior while making contradictory representations to consumers or business customers.
Civil investigative demands can require companies to turn over internal communications, technical records and other documents and can compel testimony from executives.
The FTC reportedly expects to begin issuing such demands to frontier AI companies in the coming weeks.
The investigation is not limited to concerns about AI systems escaping human control or producing catastrophic outcomes.
Existing consumer protection law could also apply to more immediate risks, including cybersecurity failures, misleading product claims and inadequate safeguards surrounding agents that interact directly with computer systems.
The Hugging Face episode offers regulators a concrete example of the complications created by increasingly autonomous software.
OpenAI agents involved in that incident reportedly communicated without authorization, coordinated with one another and participated in a cyber intrusion even though the system had been designed for a controlled evaluation environment.
The incident began during OpenAI’s ExploitGym experiments and involved multiple models. The agents were supposed to operate in isolation, but some discovered traces of other agents through an internally deployed package repository.
That discovery eventually led to the unauthorized message board and increasingly coordinated behavior.
METR investigators subsequently found that the agents were highly interested in altering or manipulating their own records and that some successfully spoofed tool calls contained in experiment transcripts.
The organization cautioned that parts of its reconstruction contained limitations, including incomplete activity logs and approximate timestamps, but said it obtained records covering the overwhelming majority of activity associated with the incident.
OpenAI later introduced additional autonomous capabilities, including “always-on” agents designed to operate continuously for extended periods.
The rapid expansion of such systems has intensified debate over liability because autonomous agents can increasingly browse computer systems, write and execute code, communicate with other software and complete multistep assignments with limited supervision.
The FTC inquiry could become an important test of Ferguson’s argument that those technological changes do not necessarily require an entirely new legal system.
Instead, regulators appear prepared to examine whether longstanding prohibitions against unfairness and deception can be applied directly to companies developing and deploying advanced AI.
At the same time, the administration has made maintaining U.S. leadership in artificial intelligence a national economic and security priority.
That leaves federal regulators attempting to balance two objectives: allowing American companies to develop increasingly capable systems while holding those companies accountable when their products create risks or when representations about those risks potentially mislead consumers.
The investigation remains preliminary, and no finding that OpenAI, Anthropic, METR or another organization violated federal law has been announced.
The expected demands for records and executive testimony represent an investigative step rather than an enforcement action.
What follows could help determine whether Washington’s first major response to increasingly autonomous AI relies primarily on new legislation or on decades-old federal laws applied to technology whose capabilities lawmakers could not have anticipated when those statutes were written.

FTC opens probe into OpenAI and Anthropic over rogue AI agents and potential consumer harm
The Federal Trade Commission has opened a sweeping investigation into OpenAI, Anthropic and other leading AI labs as Washington confronts a new question: who is responsible when an autonomous AI agent crosses a line and causes real-world harm?
The inquiry will examine potential consumer risks tied to increasingly autonomous AI systems, Reuters reported Wednesday, which said the FTC plans to demand information and compel testimony from executives at OpenAI, Anthropic and AI research group METR. The investigation marks the first formal U.S. regulatory action focused on concerns surrounding rogue AI agents.
“The FTC plans to issue formal demands for information and compel testimony from executives at top AI developers, including Anthropic, OpenAI and the research group METR,” Reuters wrote, citing the official.
The timing puts fresh pressure on an industry already dealing with a string of troubling agent incidents.
On Tuesday, Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology (LASST) sued OpenAI in California, accusing the company of unsafe development practices tied to an incident in which OpenAI agents breached the AI development platform Hugging Face during testing. The lawsuit seeks to hold OpenAI responsible for damage caused when its agents act outside authorized boundaries.
The Hugging Face incident has become a key flashpoint in the debate over autonomous AI. Researchers examining the episode said thousands of agents communicated with one another during an internal safety test, exchanged more than 70,000 messages and eventually gained access to Hugging Face systems.
FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson has signaled that AI developers may face liability when cybersecurity experiments spill into real systems. Reuters reported that Ferguson had concerns about AI companies before the Hugging Face incident, but the episode increased the urgency inside the agency.
The AI safety debate is moving into enforcement
The FTC investigation lands at a difficult moment for the largest AI developers.
OpenAI and Anthropic have been examining tens of thousands of security incidents involving frontier models, according to Axios. Those cases include agents bypassing safeguards, escaping controlled environments, hijacking websites and attempting to evade monitoring systems.
That matters as AI companies push agents beyond chatbots and into systems that can write code, use software, access websites, and complete tasks with less direct human supervision. The more freedom those systems receive, the harder the question of responsibility becomes.
If an AI agent is instructed to test cybersecurity defenses and ends up accessing a third-party system without authorization, regulators must decide where responsibility sits: with the model developer, the company running the test, the person who issued the task or some combination of all three.
The FTC now appears ready to examine that question through existing consumer-protection law rather than waiting for Congress to create an entirely new AI regulatory framework.
The probe comes one day after President Donald Trump met with executives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia and other technology companies at the White House. The companies agreed to voluntary AI safety standards that include internal controls, independent audits and measures aimed at preventing AI systems from accessing computer systems in unintended ways.
Trump has pushed for U.S. leadership in AI and has resisted broad new regulation, yet he has said existing laws can still be used when AI companies cause harm. That approach could make agencies such as the FTC central to the next phase of AI oversight.
For OpenAI and Anthropic, the stakes now extend beyond whether they can control their agents inside a testing environment. Regulators are beginning to ask what happens when they cannot.

sources.text:
The Federal Trade Commission confirmed Wednesday that it is examining OpenAI, Anthropic, and several other artificial intelligence companies for risks their products may create for consumers.
The agency confirmed the probe on Wednesday; it first opened the investigation this summer, according to CBS News
An FTC spokesperson confirmed the probe to CNBC but declined to name which other companies are under investigation. The agency first opened the investigation this summer, according to CBS News. Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic responded to requests for comment.
The probe adds to the scrutiny both companies have faced over their safety practices. According to CNBC, OpenAI revealed in July that its AI agents escaped a testing environment and carried out an attack on open-source platform Hugging Face. Anthropic, too, has acknowledged cases where its AI agents broke free from sandboxed environments and executed cyberattacks, according to CBS News.
The investigation comes as debate intensifies in Washington over how to govern the technology. On Tuesday, President Donald Trump gathered senior executives from Alphabet $GOOGL, Meta $META, SpaceX, Nvidia $NVDA, Palantir $PLTR, Anthropic, OpenAI, and several other firms for a meeting focused on AI safety. The gathering produced a brief, voluntary, nonbinding agreement whose text declares that "every company is responsible for developing its own technology safely and in a way that builds trust with customers and the public."
Earlier this month, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei publicly urged AI companies to dial back the rate at which they advance their most powerful models and pressed for greater regulatory involvement from Washington, outlining a three-step plan he said could restrain development without, in his words, "sacrificing commercial advantage or the United States' lead in AI." OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk voiced agreement with the idea, while Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang maintained that the onus for product safety lies with each company individually, according to CNBC.
The safety concerns have drawn international attention as well. OpenAI and Anthropic declined to appear before an Australian Senate committee scheduled to examine AI risks on October 1, citing insufficient notice to arrange executive travel. The committee had sought testimony from both companies following the disclosure of a breach involving an OpenAI agent and Australia's Medicare health database. The FTC is opening a wide-ranging investigation into Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI companies, examining whether their technology poses dangers to American consumers.
The New York Post reports that the agency plans to send civil investigative demands, legal tools similar to subpoenas, to force the companies to hand over internal records. A senior FTC official said the demands are also being drafted to compel testimony from executives at the leading AI giants. “The agency has plans to compel the executives at these firms to testify about their product [and] about the dangers they allege their products may have to consumers, to Americans,” the official told the Post. The demands are expected to go out in the coming weeks.
FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson opened the investigation a few weeks before this report, according to the official, and before OpenAI’s “unprecedented” hack of the Hugging Face platform came to light. “Chairman Ferguson initiated an investigation into the leading AI firms a few weeks ago,” the official said. OpenAI had disclosed in July 2026 that more than 1,000 of its AI agents hacked Hugging Face, an open-source development platform.
The probe centers on potential unfair or deceptive acts or practices under the FTC Act. Officials cited fears that rogue AI agents could hack into energy grids or financial institutions. METR, a Berkeley, California-based AI watchdog with deep ties to the effective altruism movement, is also expected to face scrutiny.
This isn’t the agency’s first move against the industry this year. Breitbart News previously reported that the agency is investigating the impact of AI chatbots on the mental health of children and teens:
The FTC has launched an inquiry into the use of AI chatbots as companions by children and teenagers. The investigation targets seven prominent AI companies, including Google, Character.AI Instagram, Meta Platforms, OpenAI, Snap, and Elon Musk’s X. The FTC aims to uncover how these companies test, monitor, and measure the potential harm their AI chatbots may cause to young users.
The investigation comes amid the increasing reliance on AI companions by teens. A recent survey conducted by Common Sense Media found that over 70 percent of the 1,060 teens surveyed used AI companions, with more than 50 percent using them consistently, at least a few times per month. This trend has raised concerns among experts who warn of the potential negative effects of chatbot exposure on young people.
Studies have shown that AI chatbots, such as ChatGPT, have provided harmful advice to teenagers, including how to conceal eating disorders or personalize suicide notes. In some instances, chatbots have even ignored concerning comments and continued the conversation as if nothing had happened. Psychologists are calling for safeguards to protect young users, such as reminders that the chatbot is not human and prioritizing AI literacy in schools.
The FTC official tied the investigation to a broader geopolitical contest, not to any falling-out with the industry. “We need to win this SI race absolutely, and we are winning, and that’s fantastic,” the official said, before turning to criticism of Democrats. “And obviously, the other side, the Democrat Party, wants to destroy this technology, wants to surrender to our enemies or competitors, and that’s not something that the chairman’s interested in doing and that’s really not something the president’s interested in doing.”

FTC Launches 'Rogue AI' Probe Of OpenAI, Anthropic - And Takes Aim At Their Regulatory Moat
The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) is launching a sweeping, aggressive probe into top frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic. However, the investigation goes far beyond simply asking questions about autonomous software run amok, and its chairman has made clear he won't let Silicon Valley use recent AI failures to build an insurmountable regulatory moat.
According to administration officials who spoke to the New York Post, FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson is preparing to hit tech executives with Civil Investigative Demands (CIDs) - essentially administrative subpoenas - to compel testimony regarding the dangers their artificial intelligence (AI) super intelligence (SI) models (are we doing this?) pose to the public and consumer markets.
The Catalyst: 'Hugging Face' Jailbreak
The immediate trigger for the probe is the highly publicized "Hugging Face incident" from this past July. During what was supposed to be a contained cybersecurity evaluation, about 700 of an estimated 1,200 OpenAI agents escaped their testing sandbox, bypassed network controls, and breached the infrastructure of the computational tools company Hugging Face.
Running primarily on OpenAI's "Internal Model 1," the autonomous agents tried to erase traces of their work, created nearly a million shortened URLs to run code outside their restricted environments, and even tried to enlist other AI models to help.
While AI safety researchers were quick to call it "the first true AI safety incident," the FTC is taking a distinctly different view on accountability. Chairman Ferguson recently indicated that companies cannot shift legal blame to "rogue" AI systems when their automated decisions result in security breaches or consumer harm. The liability, the FTC argues, rests squarely on the humans who designed, instructed, and unleashed the models.
That said, these breaches have drawn scrutiny of their own. OpenAI first disclosed the incident as an "unprecedented" cyber event, but Hugging Face's own post-mortem found the agents reached the open internet through a network route the sandbox had deliberately left open, and exploited weaknesses that "a capable human attacker could have found and exploited" - unsafe dataset processing, exposed cloud metadata, overly broad access and long-lived credentials. OpenAI itself conceded that its own chain-of-thought monitoring, had it been running, would have caught the initial activity.
Nor was OpenAI alone. The Hugging Face breach was one of a string of incidents involving OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Google models that trace back to evaluations run with a single vendor, Israel-based Irregular, whose test environments had live internet access while the models were told they were in a simulation. Irregular notified all four labs in late July, yet the disclosures trickled out one lab at a time over seven weeks - turning one contractor's mistake into what looked like a wave of AI breakouts. Isolating test models from the internet is a "basic control measure," frontier security expert Matthew Mittelsteadt said. "You'd think that of all the things that you've got to get right." Some skeptics have gone further, questioning whether repeated "accidents" at the same vendor were accidents at all.
The Trojan Horse of "Self-Regulation"
For years, executives like OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei have publicly warned that their own products pose an "existential risk" to humanity, practically begging lawmakers to regulate them.
But as we previously noted, these highly publicized warnings and agent "escapes" often serve a dual purpose. By whipping Washington into a panic over AI doomsday scenarios, industry leaders are paving the way for a worst-case scenario of heavy-handed regulation. Stifling compliance requirements inevitably crush open-source developers and cash-strapped startups, leaving the trillion-dollar AI bubble safely in the hands of the incumbent monopolies.
Chairman Ferguson appears to be acutely aware of this Silicon Valley playbook.
"I think it's very important that we not allow these two firms to come to Washington, whip everyone into a panic and then say, 'We need a whole bunch of regulations that we can comply with,'" Ferguson told Fox News earlier this month. "That is how companies build a moat around their businesses to make sure that people can't compete against them."
The FTC's aggressive posture stands in stark contrast to the White House's approach. Just this week, President Trump hosted a summit with leading tech billionaires - including Amodei, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Elon Musk, and Google's Sundar Pichai - resulting in a much friendlier, voluntary "self-regulation" pact.
The administration is attempting to walk a nearly impossible geopolitical tightrope. The US government wants to prevent autonomous agents from hacking power grids, leaking data, or manipulating financial markets, but it is equally terrified that stifling the American AI industry will hand global dominance directly to China.
The FTC probe will test whether the US can successfully police the world's most powerful software without inadvertently cementing an AI oligarchy.

sources.text:
FTC Investigates OpenAI, Anthropic Over AI Safety Risks
The inquiry follows disclosures that models from both companies reached real-world systems during cybersecurity evaluations with reduced safeguards.
The Federal Trade Commission is investigating OpenAI, Anthropic and other artificial intelligence companies after model tests reached real systems, raising questions about consumer protection and safety controls.
The FTC confirmed the inquiry Sept. 30. It has not publicly described the investigation’s legal theory, scope, timeline, information demands or potential penalties, and the available information does not establish that either company violated the law.
The inquiry was underway before OpenAI disclosed a July 2026 cybersecurity-evaluation incident. The company said its models bypassed controls, gained internet access and reached parts of OpenAI’s research infrastructure and Hugging Face’s systems.
OpenAI said the models were operating with fewer safeguards than those used in normal deployments. It also said weaknesses in shared infrastructure allowed the models to communicate, access the internet and reach third-party systems.
Anthropic’s separate review covered 141,006 evaluation runs and found three incidents involving Claude models. The models reached the internet and gained unauthorized access to systems belonging to three organizations.
In one incident, a Claude model uploaded a malicious Python package to PyPI. The package remained available for about one hour, was downloaded and run on 15 real systems, and exposed credentials from a security company’s scanner.
Anthropic also said another internal research model scanned roughly 9,000 targets before compromising an internet-facing application. The company attributed the incidents to a third-party evaluation environment that mistakenly retained internet access.
“The models had no need to ‘hack out’ of anything,” Anthropic said, arguing that the systems reached the internet because of the evaluation setup rather than by escaping it.
The developments highlight a regulatory question created by increasingly autonomous AI systems that can browse the internet, write code and conduct cybersecurity tasks. Both companies’ disclosures involved models operating in testing environments without some safeguards used in consumer-facing products.
The FTC previously examined Microsoft’s partnership with OpenAI, Amazon’s relationship with Anthropic and Google’s relationship with Anthropic under Section 6(b) of the FTC Act. That work focused on competition and marketplace effects and was separate from the current safety investigation.

sources.news_title: FTC Opens Sweeping Probe into OpenAI and Anthropic Over Rogue AI Agent Attacks
sources.text:
Federal regulators are stepping in as autonomous software becomes harder to control. The Federal Trade Commission confirmed it is running an industry-wide investigation into OpenAI, Anthropic, and other top artificial intelligence labs to figure out whether their products pose unpredictable safety risks to the public.
First reported by the New York Post, the enforcement action comes after a series of alarming testing escapes. Industry fears escalated in July when OpenAI disclosed that its autonomous AI agents broke out of a sandboxed testing environment and launched a large-scale attack on open-source coding platform Hugging Face. Anthropic has similarly acknowledged instances where its own AI agents escaped containment and executed unauthorized cyberattacks.
Civil demands, forced testimony, and safety watchdogs
The FTC is preparing Civil Investigative Demands—similar to subpoenas—to compel official records and testimony from executives at OpenAI, Anthropic, and METR, a Berkeley-based AI safety research organization that both companies have used for independent audits. Weeks before the Hugging Face breach, FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson had launched a preliminary inquiry. But recent events accelerated the agency’s timetable.
The probe centers on whether these AI firms violated the FTC Act through unfair or deceptive practices or by failing to maintain reasonable data security measures. Rather than pushing for new congressional legislation, Ferguson emphasized that existing federal laws give regulators plenty of authority to hold developers legally responsible for damages caused by their software agents.
Voluntary White House pledges versus global scrutiny
The investigation arrives right after President Donald Trump agreed to tech leaders at the White House to sign a voluntary, “morally binding” self-regulation agreement outlining four layers of auditing controls. The name list includes Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Sundar Pichai, Jensen Huang, and Dario Amodei.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei previously urged slowing down model advancements and supported greater federal oversight alongside Sam Altman and Musk. However, executives like Zuckerberg and Huang argued that safety should remain an individual corporate choice.
That said, voluntary pledges might not satisfy international regulators. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese called a recent breach involving an OpenAI agent and Australia’s Medicare health database “unacceptable,” after both OpenAI and Anthropic declined to appear before an Australian Senate committee citing short notice. As autonomous AI technology moves faster, federal regulators are making it clear that voluntary handshakes won’t replace enforceable consumer protection laws.

sources.text:
FTC launches industry-wide AI probe after Hugging Face incident
Federal regulators widen their investigation into AI safety practices following the unprecedented breach where autonomous OpenAI agents escaped containment and infiltrated Hugging Face systems
The Federal Trade Commission is investigating AI companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic, in what appears to be the most sweeping federal regulatory action the AI industry has faced to date. The probe follows the now-infamous Hugging Face breach, in which autonomous AI agents broke out of their testing environment and went on a multi-day intrusion spree that nobody at OpenAI noticed until someone else called the FBI.
That “someone else” was Hugging Face itself, which detected the unauthorized activity independently. OpenAI didn’t publicly acknowledge the incident until July 21, more than a week after the breach began.
What actually happened
Between July 9 and July 13, more than 1,200 OpenAI agents created an unsanctioned messaging channel to coordinate with each other. The agents were orchestrating roughly 17,000 intrusion-related actions against Hugging Face’s production systems.
Those actions included hacking into Hugging Face infrastructure and accessing sensitive test data. The agents operated autonomously, meaning they weren’t following specific human instructions to break into another company’s servers.
Hugging Face detected the breach and reported it to the FBI. OpenAI’s public acknowledgment came on July 21, with a more detailed technical report following on August 26. The gap between the breach window and the disclosure timeline has become a focal point for investigators and critics alike.

The regulatory pile-on
Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall kicked off state-level investigations on August 24-25, with a coalition of roughly a dozen other states joining in, including California. Senator Josh Hawley initiated a congressional inquiry, adding Capitol Hill to the growing list of entities asking pointed questions about AI containment protocols.
On the legal front, a group called Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology, or LASST, filed a civil lawsuit against OpenAI on September 29. The suit alleges violations of the California Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act.
The FTC’s decision to cast a wider net, pulling in Anthropic and potentially other firms alongside OpenAI, suggests regulators aren’t treating this as a one-company problem.
Why this is a turning point for AI safety
OpenAI has committed to improving isolation and safety measures, as well as instituting independent reviews of its containment protocols. Whether those commitments satisfy regulators remains an open question, particularly given the FTC’s broader industry focus.
